questions.q: What is the literal meaning of the Bundelkhandi phrase 'पैक डकस डकस वपंजु न पुखरह' as used in the poem's opening line?
questions.a: The phrase literally translates to 'The dark, dark letters do not bloom/read' — 'पैक' means father, 'डकस डकस' means dark/dark (referring to the black ink of letters), 'वपंजु' is a dialect form of 'पढ़ते' (read), and 'पुखरह' means bloom/sprout/succeed. A wrong answer (e.g., 'The father does not like dark colors') reveals the student is treating the dialect as decorative rather than as a carrier of the father's lived reality and oral culture.

questions.q: Explain in your own words why the father says 'ड्यडक्स इज क्त्ज फ्क्जस' (Don't cast your eyes on the threshold) when the son urges him to become literate.
questions.a: The threshold (देहली) symbolizes the boundary between the father's familiar, oral world of labor and the alien, written world of bureaucracy that the son inhabits. By saying 'don't cast eyes on the threshold,' the father rejects not literacy per se, but the son's assumption that crossing that threshold will automatically bring dignity — he knows the written world still discriminates against his kind. A wrong answer focusing only on 'stubbornness' misses the poem's critique of institutional exclusion.

questions.q: Apply the concept of 'dramatic irony' to the moment when the son says 'पैक] रक ी<+ य्सुक वपंजु ग्स' (Father, reading is good) and the father replies 'इक रक्स द्गा फ्क्स... इक रक्स द्गा फ्क्स' (I say no... I say no). How does the reader know more than the son?
questions.a: Step 1: Identify the son's premise — literacy equals progress. Step 2: Identify the father's lived experience — he has seen literate people (like the 'क्चक च्क्क') still exploit the illiterate. Step 3: The irony: the son thinks he is giving the father a key; the father knows the lock is rigged. Step 4: The reader sees both perspectives because the poem gives us the father's interior monologue ('इक रक्स कह द्गा...'). A wrong answer that only defines dramatic irony without mapping it to these specific lines shows inability to apply literary terms to dialect texts.

questions.q: Analyze how the poet uses the recurring image of 'डकस' (dark/black) — in 'डकस डकस', 'डकस फुखक्सा' (black letters), 'डकस फ्प्किक्सा' (black pages) — to structure the poem's argument about knowledge systems.
questions.a: The image evolves: initially 'डकस डकस' = opaque, impenetrable script (stanza 1); then 'डकस फुखक्सा' = the physical tools of a power the father cannot access (stanza 2); finally 'डकस फ्प्किक्सा' = the bureaucratic records that ultimately dispossess people like him (stanza 4). The darkness is not ignorance but a different epistemology — oral, tactile, memory-based. A wrong answer that treats 'dark' as a static symbol of illiteracy fails to track the poet's subversion of the light/dark binary.

questions.q: Evaluate the claim: "The poem ultimately sides with the son because the father agrees to learn in the last stanza ('पैक इकुस वपंजु ग्स... इक रक्स द्गा क्कि पैक] रक ी<+ य्सुक')." Defend or refute using textual evidence.
questions.a: Refute. The father's agreement ('इक रक्स द्गा क्कि पैक] रक ी<+ य्सुक' — 'Okay, I'll read') comes only after he extracts a promise: 'ड्यडक्स इज क्त्ज फ्क्जस' (don't look at the threshold) and 'ड्यडक्स इक कह द्गा न त्कुस न्वहख्स' (I will never go to the city). He learns on his terms, not the son's. The poem ends with the father retaining his autonomy ('ड्यडक्स इक कह द्गा न त्कुस न्वहख्स त्क ड्यडक्क्स इज क्त्ज फ्क्जस'). A wrong answer that calls this a 'happy resolution' ignores the conditional, resistant nature of the father's consent.

questions.q: Create a 2-minute monologue from the perspective of the 'क्चक च्क्क' (the literate exploiter mentioned in stanza 3) justifying why he keeps the father's thumb-print on blank papers. Use at least two Bundelkhandi phrases from the poem.
questions.a: A strong monologue would capture the exploiter's bureaucratic rationality: 'These thumb-prints (अंगूठा) are safer than signatures — they don't tremble, they don't question. I write "डकस फ्प्किक्सा" (black pages) for their own good; the city courts only read ink, not soil.' It must use 'अंगूठा' and 'डकस फ्प्किक्सा' organically. A weak answer makes him a cartoon villain; a strong one shows how literacy itself becomes a weapon in his mouth.
